title: To Be Versus to Seem
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by an article on AI titled "Subcontracting Our Minds" and its invocation of Rousseau's distinction between "being" and "seeming," Stuart reflects on a Thanksgiving-week question he keeps posing to his students: do you want to actually be a stronger thinker, reader, writer, and person, or just seem like one? He connects this to Warren Buffett's "inner scorecard" concept and a Ben Okri quote about the power of the stories we tell ourselves, tying both back to the central thesis of The Will to Learn -- that all students want to want to learn, even when they act indifferent. The essay is personal and reflective, framing the daily grind of mini-sermons and Woodenization as slow, patient seed-planting in students' hearts rather than a fast-acting technique. Stuart closes by urging readers to use the holiday to tell themselves more grateful, hopeful stories about their own teaching labor.
points: Central framing device: Rousseau's "to be or to seem" distinction, applied to students' daily choice about whether to actually grow or merely appear to be trying.
He pairs this with Warren Buffett's "inner scorecard" concept, reframing the same idea in terms teachers can use directly with students who care more about visible effort than real growth.

Stuart explicitly reaffirms The Will to Learn's central thesis -- that all students want to want to learn -- as the emotional anchor that keeps him patient through indifferent-seeming classroom responses.
The Ben Okri quote about self-told stories is used to argue that teachers' own narrative about their work shapes their resilience as much as any external circumstance.
quotes: Though I found the author's arguments compelling, what I loved most was his surfacing of an old Rousseau argument that it is necessary "to be or to seem.
The big question about how people behave is whether they've got an Inner Scorecard or an Outer Scorecard. It helps if you can be satisfied with an Inner Scorecard.

It seems to me that in my classes this year, I am continually drawn to putting this question before my students: Would you like to be a stronger, more capable, more agile thinker, reader, writer, speaker, person…or do you just want to keep doing just enough to seem like one?
Beware the stories you read or tell; subtly, at night, beneath the waters of consciousness, they are altering your world.

A story I've had to remind myself of too many times to count this school year is that my students want to want to be stronger students. When I keep trying to cast a vision for them, to Woodenize effective learning and living for them, to define success in a "no top to the mountain" kind of way…I'm patiently planting seeds they want to take root in their hearts and minds.
It is hard work, cultivating care in the hearts of human beings. But in the end, it does produce fruit if we do not give up.
